# Correction: The manifold structure of limb coordination in walking Drosophila

## Authors

- Brian D DeAngelis ([ORCID: 0000-0001-9418-7619](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9418-7619))
- Jacob A Zavatone-Veth ([ORCID: 0000-0002-4060-1738](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4060-1738))
- Damon A Clark ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8487-700X](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8487-700X)) †

† Corresponding author

## Template-matching suggests an absence of canonical tetrapod and wave gaits

We next sought to systematically investigate how closely our data matched the configurations of relative limb phasing specified by each of the canonical gaits. To do so, we defined a template-matching coherence metric based on a simple model for networks of coupled oscillators (see Materials and methods). The coherence falls between zero and one, with unity corresponding to an exact match to the template phase configuration. The tripod coherence distribution is sharply peaked around ~0.9, indicating a close template match, while the distributions for the other canonical gaits were broader and peaked at lower coherences (Figure 3H). If the fly preferentially used different gaits at different forward walking speeds, then we would expect to see a peak in the conditional coherence distribution for a given canonical gait at some characteristic forward velocity. Yet, we did not observe any such distinct peaks in our data (Figure 3I). At all but the lowest speeds, the most coherent phase template is tripod (Figure 3J). Furthermore, the coherences in non-tripod modes are quite low, even among those instances better described by canonical gaits other than tripod (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Therefore, under an analysis designed to sensitively compare our data to canonical gait configurations, we do not observe significant evidence for the use of canonical tetrapod and wave gaits.

Corrected section of text:

## Template-matching suggests little evidence for preferred canonical tetrapod and wave gaits

We next sought to systematically investigate how closely our data matched the configurations of relative limb phasing specified by each of the canonical gaits. To do so, we defined a template-matching coherence metric based on a simple model for networks of coupled oscillators (see Materials and methods). The coherence falls between zero and one, with unity corresponding to an exact match to the template phase configuration. The tripod coherence distribution is sharply peaked around ~0.9, indicating a close template match, while the distributions for the other canonical gaits were broader and peaked at lower coherences (Figure 3H). If the fly preferentially used different gaits at different forward walking speeds, then we would expect to see a peak in the conditional coherence distribution for a given canonical gait at some characteristic forward velocity. Yet, there were not prominent peaks in our data, and all coherences yielded low average values at slow walking speeds (Figure 3I). At those slower speeds, where mean coherences were low, the tetrapod coherences became more likely to be the highest coherence (Figure 3J). This is consistent with the observation of tetrapod-like coordination patterns at low speeds (Figure 3F–﻿G), and with the increased spread of the distribution of relative phases at low speeds (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—﻿figure supplements 2 and 3; Wosnitza et al., 2013). However, even when the largest coherence was not tripod, these non-tripod coherences were lower than when the tripod coherence was largest (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). Since the tetrapod coherence of a perfect tripod gait is 3–1/2 ~ 0.6, this coherence metric may not show strong contrasts under some deformations in coordination. Therefore, under these analyses, we do not observe strong evidence for the preferred use of canonical tetrapod and wave gaits.

results.result: The authors developed a template-matching coherence metric based on a coupled oscillator model to quantify how closely observed limb coordination matches canonical gait templates. The metric ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect match to a template phase configuration.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 describe a methodological development that is clearly stated and mathematically well-defined. The metric's properties (range and interpretation) are explicitly defined, and the approach is referenced to Materials and methods for implementation details.

results.result: Analysis of coherence distributions shows that tripod gait has a sharply peaked distribution around 0.9 coherence indicating close template match, while other canonical gaits (tetrapod, wave) show broader distributions peaked at lower coherences.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 are directly supported by Figure 3H showing the coherence distributions. The tripod gait shows distinctly higher and more concentrated coherence values compared to other canonical gaits, providing clear quantitative evidence for the dominance of tripod coordination.

results.result: The conditional coherence distributions across walking speeds do not show prominent peaks characteristic of preferential gait usage at specific speeds. At all but the lowest speeds, tripod is the most coherent phase template, though all coherences show low average values at slow walking speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C16 are supported by Figures 3I and 3J. The absence of distinct peaks in conditional coherence distributions (C7) contradicts the expectation (C6) that would arise if flies preferentially used different gaits at different speeds. The corrected figures show this pattern clearly, with tripod dominance except at lowest speeds.

results.result: At slow walking speeds where mean coherences are low, tetrapod coherences become more likely to be the highest coherence. This observation is consistent with tetrapod-like coordination patterns and increased spread of relative phase distributions at low speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by multiple figures (3F-G, 3D-E, 3J, and supplements 2-3) and citation to Wosnitza et al., 2013. The corrected Figure 3J clearly shows increased tetrapod coherence at low speeds, and this is appropriately contextualized with prior observations of phase variability at slow speeds.

results.result: Even when non-tripod gaits show the highest coherence, these coherence values are lower than when tripod coherence is highest. Non-tripod mode coherences remain quite low even among instances best described by canonical gaits other than tripod.
results.evaluation: Claims C12 and C17 are supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3 (both original and corrected versions). This finding indicates that even when alternative gaits appear to be used, they do not match their canonical templates as closely as tripod gait matches its template.

results.result: The tetrapod coherence of a perfect tripod gait is mathematically 3^(-1/2) ≈ 0.6, which means the coherence metric may not show strong contrasts under some deformations in coordination.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C14 present a mathematical property and its implication for metric sensitivity. The calculation is correct (3^(-1/2) ≈ 0.577), and the authors appropriately acknowledge this as a limitation of their metric. This cross-sensitivity between gait templates is an important caveat for interpretation.

results.result: The template-matching analyses do not provide strong evidence for the preferred use of canonical tetrapod and wave gaits in Drosophila walking.
results.evaluation: Claims C15 and C18 represent the main conclusion, which is appropriately supported by the collective evidence from claims C3-C12 and C17. The corrected version (C15) uses more cautious language ('strong evidence' vs 'significant evidence') that better reflects the nuanced findings, particularly the metric limitation noted in C13-C14 and the low coherence values for non-tripod gaits even when they are highest.
